blocks.p: But now, as Shaddai would have it, there was a man named Mr. Watch-well, a great lover of the people of Mansoul. As was his habit, he went listening up and down in Mansoul to learn, if he could, whether there was any design against it. For he was always a jealous, watchful man, and feared that some mischief would befall the town sometime, either from the Diabolonians within or from some power outside. Now it happened one time, as Mr. Watch-well went listening here and there, that he came upon a place in Mansoul called Vilehill, where Diabolonians used to meet. Hearing a muttering (it was night, you must understand), he crept softly closer to listen. He had not stood long under the end of a house there before he heard someone confidently declare that it would not be long before Diabolus took possession of Mansoul again; and that then the Diabolonians intended to put all Mansoulians to the sword, to kill and destroy the King’s captains, and to drive all his soldiers out of the town. The speaker said, moreover, that he knew Diabolus had more than twenty thousand fighting men ready for this design, and that it would not be months before they all saw it.

Mr. Watch-well quickly believed this story was true, so he went straight to the Lord Mayor’s house and told him; and the Lord Mayor sent for the town’s own preacher and broke the matter to him. The preacher at once raised the alarm, for he was now the chief preacher in Mansoul, since the Lord Secretary, whom they had grieved, was still ill at ease with them. He did it this way: that same hour he had the lecture bell rung, and the people came together. Then he gave them a short exhortation to watchfulness, and made Mr. Watch-well’s news his subject. “For,” he said, “a horrible plot has been contrived against Mansoul, to massacre us all in a single day. Nor is this story to be taken lightly, for it comes from Mr. Watch-well, who has always been a lover of Mansoul, a sober and sensible man, no gossip or spreader of false reports, but one who loves to look into the very bottom of things, and who speaks of no news except on very solid grounds.

“I will call him, and you will hear him for yourselves.” So he called him, and Mr. Watch-well came and told his tale so precisely, and backed its truth with such ample grounds, that Mansoul was soon convinced of it. The preacher also backed him up. “Sirs,” he said, “it is not unreasonable for us to believe it. We have provoked Shaddai to anger, and have sinned Emmanuel out of the town. We have had too much to do with Diabolonians, and have forsaken our former mercies. No wonder, then, if the enemy both within and without should scheme and plot our ruin; and what time could be better for it than this? The sickness is in the town now, and we have been made weak by it. Many a well-meaning man is dead, and lately the Diabolonians grow stronger and stronger.

“Besides,” said the preacher, “I have received this one further hint from this good teller of truth: he understood from those he overheard that several letters have lately passed between the furies and the Diabolonians, aimed at our destruction.”

When Mansoul heard all this and could not deny it, they lifted up their voices and wept. Mr. Watch-well also confirmed, in front of the townsmen, everything their preacher had said. So they set themselves afresh to lament their folly, and to double their petitions to Shaddai and his Son. They also broke the matter to the captains, high commanders, and men of war in the town, begging them to use every means to be strong and take good courage, to look to their armor, and to make themselves ready to give Diabolus battle by night and by day, if he should come, as they were told he would, to besiege the town.

When the captains heard this, being always true lovers of the town of Mansoul, what did they do but shake themselves like so many Samsons and come together to consult and contrive how to defeat those bold and hellish schemes that Diabolus and his friends had set in motion against the now sickly, weak, and much impoverished town of Mansoul? And they agreed on the following points:

1. That the gates of Mansoul should be kept shut and fastened with bars and locks, and that all persons going out or coming in should be very strictly examined by the captains of the guards. “So that,” they said, “those among us who are managing the plot may be caught, coming or going; and so that we may also find out who the chief contrivers of our ruin among us are.”

2. Next, that a strict search should be made for every kind of Diabolonian throughout the whole town of Mansoul; and that every man’s house should be looked into from top to bottom, house by house, so that, if possible, more might be discovered of all among them who had a hand in these designs.

3. It was further concluded that wherever, or with whomever, any Diabolonians were found, those townspeople of Mansoul who had given them house and shelter should do penance in the public square, to their own shame and as a warning to others.

4. It was resolved, moreover, by the famous town of Mansoul, that a public fast and day of humiliation should be kept throughout the whole town, to vindicate their Prince, and to humble themselves before him for their offenses against him and against Shaddai his Father. It was further resolved that any in Mansoul who did not try on that day to keep the fast and humble themselves for their faults, but minded their worldly business or were found wandering up and down the streets, should be taken for Diabolonians and suffer as Diabolonians for their wicked conduct.

5. It was further concluded that, with all the speed and warmth of heart they could, they would renew their humiliation for sin and their petitions to Shaddai for help. They also resolved to send word to the court of everything Mr. Watch-well had told them.

6. It was also determined that Mansoul should thank Mr. Watch-well for diligently seeking the town’s welfare; and further, since he was so naturally inclined to seek their good and to undermine their enemies, they gave him a commission as scout-master-general, for the town’s good.

When the town and its captains had concluded this, they did as they had said. They shut their gates; they made strict search for Diabolonians; they made those with whom any were found do penance in the public square; they kept their fast and renewed their petitions to their Prince. And Mr. Watch-well carried out his charge, and the trust Mansoul had put in his hands, with great conscience and faithfulness; for he gave himself wholly to his work, not only within the town, but going out as well to look, and see, and hear.

Not many days afterward he made ready for a journey and went toward Hell-Gate Hill, into the country where the Doubters were. There he heard of everything that had been talked about in Mansoul, and saw too that Diabolus was almost ready to march. So he came back with speed, called the captains and elders of Mansoul together, and told them where he had been, what he had heard, and what he had seen. In particular he told them that Diabolus had made old Mr. Incredulity, the one who once broke out of prison in Mansoul, the general of his army; that his army was made up entirely of Doubters, and that their number was more than twenty thousand. He told them, moreover, that Diabolus intended to bring the chief princes of the infernal pit with him, and to make them chief captains over his Doubters; and that it was certainly true that several of the black den would ride with Diabolus as volunteers, to bring Mansoul back under the rule of Diabolus.

He said, moreover, that he understood from the Doubters he had been among that the reason old Incredulity had been made general of the whole army was that none was more loyal to the tyrant than he, and that he had an unappeasable spite against the welfare of the town of Mansoul. “Besides,” he said, “he remembers the insults Mansoul has given him, and he is resolved to be revenged on them.

“But the black princes are to be made high commanders, only Incredulity is to be over them all; because (and this I had almost forgotten) he can besiege the town of Mansoul more easily and more skillfully than any of the princes besides.”

When the captains and elders had heard Mr. Watch-well’s news, they thought it best, without further delay, to put into effect the laws their Prince had made against the Diabolonians and commanded them to enforce. So a diligent and impartial search was made at once in every house in Mansoul for every kind of Diabolonian, and two were found, in the houses of Mr. Mind and of the great Lord Willbewill. In Mr. Mind’s house was found one Lord Covetousness, but he had changed his name to Prudent-thrifty. In my Lord Willbewill’s house was found one Lasciviousness, but he had changed his name to Harmless-mirth. The captains and elders took these two and committed them to the custody of Mr. Trueman the jailer; and this man handled them so severely, and loaded them so well with irons, that in time they both fell into a deep wasting sickness and died in the prison. Their masters too, by the agreement of the captains and elders, were brought to do penance in the public square, to their shame and as a warning to the rest of the town.

Now this was the manner of penance in those days: the offenders, being made aware of the evil of what they had done, were required to confess their faults openly and to make a strict amendment of their lives.

After this, the captains and elders of Mansoul tried to find out still more Diabolonians wherever they lurked, whether in dens, caves, holes, vaults, or anywhere else in or around the wall or town. But though they could plainly see their footprints, and so follow them by their track and scent to their holds, right up to the mouths of their caves and dens, yet take them, hold them, and bring them to justice they could not; their ways were so crooked, their holds so strong, and they so quick to take refuge there.

But Mansoul now ruled the Diabolonians who were left with so firm a hand that they were glad to shrink into corners. There was a time when they dared to walk openly, and by day; but now they were forced to keep to secrecy and the night. There was a time when a Mansoulian was their companion; but now they counted the Mansoulians deadly enemies. This good change was made in the famous town of Mansoul by Mr. Watch-well’s intelligence.

By this time Diabolus had finished raising the army he intended to bring with him for the ruin of Mansoul, and had set over them captains and other field officers who best suited his furious temper. He himself was lord paramount; Incredulity was general of his army; their highest captains will be named later. But now for their officers, their colors, and their scutcheons, the emblems borne on their shields:

1. Their first captain was Captain Rage. He was captain over the Election-doubters, who doubt that God has chosen them. His were the red colors; his standard-bearer was Mr. Destructive; and he had the great red dragon for his scutcheon.

2. The second captain was Captain Fury. He was captain over the Calling-doubters, who doubt that God has truly called them. His standard-bearer was Mr. Darkness; his colors were the pale ones; and he had the fiery flying serpent for his scutcheon.

3. The third captain was Captain Damnation. He was captain over the Grace-doubters, who doubt God’s free grace toward them. His were the red colors; Mr. No-Life carried them; and he had the black den for his scutcheon.

4. The fourth captain was Captain Insatiable. He was captain over the Faith-doubters, who doubt that their faith is true faith. His were the red colors; Mr. Devourer carried them; and he had the yawning jaws for his scutcheon.

5. The fifth captain was Captain Brimstone. He was captain over the Perseverance-doubters, who doubt that God will keep them to the end. His too were the red colors; Mr. Burning carried them; and his scutcheon was the blue and stinking flame.

6. The sixth captain was Captain Torment. He was captain over the Resurrection-doubters, who doubt that the dead will rise. His colors were the pale ones; Mr. Gnaw was his standard-bearer; and he had the black worm for his scutcheon.

7. The seventh captain was Captain No-Ease. He was captain over the Salvation-doubters, who doubt that they will be saved. His were the red colors; Mr. Restless carried them; and his scutcheon was the ghastly picture of death.

8. The eighth captain was Captain Sepulchre. He was captain over the Glory-doubters, who doubt the glory to come. His too were the pale colors; Mr. Corruption was his standard-bearer; and he had for his scutcheon a skull and dead men’s bones.

9. The ninth captain was Captain Past-Hope. He was captain of those called the Felicity-doubters, who doubt the everlasting happiness of heaven. His standard-bearer was Mr. Despair; his too were the red colors; and his scutcheon was a hot iron and the hard heart.

These were his captains, and these their forces; these were their standards, these their colors, and these their scutcheons. Over these the great Diabolus set superior captains, seven in number: namely, the Lord Beelzebub, the Lord Lucifer, the Lord Legion, the Lord Apollyon, the Lord Python, the Lord Cerberus, and the Lord Belial. These seven he set over the captains; Incredulity was lord-general; and Diabolus was king. The volunteers, too, such as were like themselves, were made some of them captains of hundreds and some captains of more. And so the army of Incredulity was complete.

So they set out from Hell-Gate Hill, for that was where they mustered, and from there they marched straight toward Mansoul. Now, as I hinted before, the town had, as Shaddai would have it, received the alarm of their coming beforehand from the mouth of Mr. Watch-well. So they set a strong watch at the gates and doubled their guards. They also mounted their slings in good places, where they could conveniently hurl their great stones to harass their furious enemy.

Nor could the Diabolonians inside the town do the harm they had been meant to do, for Mansoul was awake now. But alas, poor people! They were sorely frightened at the first sight of their foes, and when the enemy sat down before the town, and especially when they heard the roaring of their drum. To tell the truth, that was astonishingly hideous to hear; it frightened everyone for seven miles around, if only they were awake and heard it. The streaming of their colors was terrible and disheartening to see, too.

When Diabolus came up against the town, he first made his approach to Ear-gate and assaulted it furiously, supposing, it seems, that his friends in Mansoul were ready to do their work within. But the vigilance of the captains had taken care of that beforehand. So, missing the help he expected from them, and finding his army warmly received by the stones the slingers slung (for I will say this for the captains: considering the weakness still on them from the long sickness in Mansoul, they behaved gallantly), he was forced to fall back somewhat from Mansoul, and to entrench himself and his men in the field, out of reach of the town’s slings.

Having entrenched himself, he threw up four mounds against the town. The first he called Mount Diabolus, putting his own name on it to frighten Mansoul the more; the other three he called Mount Alecto, Mount Megaera, and Mount Tisiphone, for these are the names of the dreadful Furies of hell. So he began to play his game with Mansoul, and to treat it as the lion treats his prey, to make it fall before his terror. But, as I said, the captains and soldiers resisted so stoutly, and did such execution with their stones, that they made him retreat, much against his will; and so Mansoul began to take courage.

Now on Mount Diabolus, which was raised on the north side of the town, the tyrant set up his standard, and it was a fearful thing to see. For by devilish art he had worked into it, in the manner of a scutcheon, a blazing flame, terrible to look at, with the picture of Mansoul burning in it.

Then Diabolus ordered his drummer to approach the walls of Mansoul every night and beat for a parley; at night, because in the daytime the slings harassed him. For the tyrant said he had a mind to parley with the now trembling town, and he had the drums beat every night so that, through sheer weariness, the townspeople might at last be forced to it, if possible, though at first they were unwilling.

So this drummer did as he was ordered: he got up and beat his drum. But when his drum sounded, if anyone looked toward the town of Mansoul, “behold, darkness and sorrow, and the light darkened in its skies.” [Isa. 5:30] No noise was ever heard on earth more terrible, except the voice of Shaddai when he speaks. And how Mansoul trembled! She now expected nothing but to be swallowed up at once.

When this drummer had beaten for a parley, he made this speech to Mansoul: “My master has told me to say to you that if you will submit willingly, you will have the good things of the earth; but if you are stubborn, he is resolved to take you by force.” But by the time the runaway had finished beating his drum, the people of Mansoul had gone to the captains in the castle, so that no one heeded the drummer or answered him. So he went no further that night, but returned to his master in the camp.

When Diabolus saw that he could not bring Mansoul to his will by drumming, the next night he sent his drummer without his drum, still to let the townsmen know that he had a mind to parley with them. But when all was said and done, his parley turned into a summons to the town to surrender; and they gave him neither attention nor a hearing, for they remembered what it had cost them at first to listen to a few words from him.
The next night he sent again, and who should his messenger to Mansoul be this time but the terrible Captain Sepulchre? He came up to the walls of Mansoul and made this speech to the town:

“You inhabitants of the rebellious town of Mansoul! I summon you in the name of the Prince Diabolus to open the gates of your town without any more ado and let the great lord come in. But if you still rebel, then when we have taken the town by force, we will swallow you up like the grave. So if you will listen to my summons, say so; and if not, let me know.

“The reason for this summons of mine,” he said, “is that my lord is your undoubted prince and lord, as you yourselves once acknowledged. Nor will the assault that was made on my lord, when Emmanuel dealt so dishonorably with him, make him give up his right and refrain from trying to recover what is his own. Consider, then, O Mansoul: will you show yourself peaceable or not? If you quietly give yourself up, then our old friendship will be renewed; but if you still refuse and rebel, then expect nothing but fire and sword.”
When the languishing town of Mansoul had heard this summoner and his summons, they were even more downcast, but they gave the captain no answer at all; so he went away as he had come.
